chapter_theme: Renunciation, argued from impermanence: the wise see that home, youth, wealth and pleasure do not last and that pleasure is mixed with pain, so they leave household life without delay, keep their vows under hardship, pity those who insult them, and master the senses to reach release.
structure_note: 54 and 60 share their second line and make nearly the same argument. 52 and 53 both name the best of people (தலையாயார்) as those who act on impermanence; 57 to 59 turn from the reasons for renouncing to the conduct of those who have renounced.

51.reading: As darkness dies when a lamp comes in, sin cannot stand before a person's austerity; and as darkness rushes back when the lamp's oil runs out, evil settles in once good deeds are exhausted.
51.nuance: The second half limits the first: austerity protects only while the merit that feeds it lasts, so the lamp makes merit something burned up, not something owned.

positions.position: Austerity here stands for the whole way of renunciation.

52.reading: The best of people reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do the work that is truly theirs; none are more foolish than the madmen who prattle endlessly of சத்தம் and astrology.
52.nuance: The target is not learning as such but study that never ends, pursued in place of what death makes urgent. 'Their own work' (தங்கருமம்) echoes Kural 266, which Mudaliar quotes.

positions.position: 'Their own work' is austerity, and the endless lore is grammar and mathematics or astrology, tool-sciences studied for a lifetime instead of the way of renunciation.
positions.quote: தங் கருமம்-தமக்கு உறுதியைச் செய்யுந் தொழிலாகிய தவத்தையே

positions.position: The wise do the good deeds fitting for them, and the endless lore is Vedic sastra and astrology.
positions.quote: மேலோர் தமக்கேற்ற நல்வினைகளைச் செய்வர். எனவே, வேத சாத்திரம், சோதிடம் என்றெல்லாம் பிதற்றுகிற

53.reading: Seeing that home, youth, beauty, high repute, wealth and strength all fail to last, the best of people, considering slowly, renounce them without delay so as to save themselves.
53.nuance: மெல்ல and நெடியார் pull two ways: the examination is unhurried, the renouncing is not. Mudaliar keeps both, glossing one as deliberate inquiry and the other as acting without delay.

54.reading: Fools, after many days of suffering, still long for a single day's pleasure; the full and settled, discerning pleasure for what it is and seeing its pain, keep off the household way.
54.nuance: The verse names household life (மனையாறு) as what the wise leave, which makes it a direct answer to the Kural's defence of the householder.

positions.position: The wise weigh, impartially, how small household pleasure is.
The wise see that pleasure comes only now and then, a little at a time, and pain is the greater part.

55.reading: The speaker tells his own heart that youth has passed to no purpose and disease and old age are coming now, and asks it to stop going its own way and set out with him on the good path.
55.nuance: The heart is treated as a separate, wayward party to be persuaded, not commanded. Mudaliar takes the good path to be release through renunciation; Shanmuganar says only 'a good way'.

56.reading: Even if a wife lacks good qualities and bears no children, the husband cannot put her away; because marriage brings this hardship, the learned gave it the name கடி.
56.nuance: The argument turns on a pun, since கடி means both marriage and 'shun'. The verse finds no fault in marriage to a good wife; it argues from the worst case that the bond, once made, can't be undone.

positions.position: The word கடி has both senses, marriage and removal, and the poet invents a reason for the name, a figure Mudaliar calls நிருக்தி.
positions.quote: 'கடி' என்னுஞ் சொற்கு 'மணம்' 'நீக்கு' ஆகிய இரண்டு பொருள்க ளுண்டு.

57.reading: When unbearable troubles come that would break the vows they took on with zeal, those who push the troubles aside and hold the vows firm are the blessed ones who guard good conduct.

58.reading: Bearing contempt is not enough: the worthy also grieve for those who scorned them, fearing that the deed will drop them into the fiery hell.
58.nuance: The pity looks to the offender's future, not to one's own injury, so forbearance becomes a form of compassion. Parimelazhagar cites this quatrain when glossing Kural 157.

59.reading: One who has the strength to guard and steer, without wavering, the craving that enters through the five gates named body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears will surely reach release.
59.nuance: The senses are called five mouths (ஐவாய) through which craving feeds; the verse asks for them to be steered, not destroyed.

60.reading: Fools, though they see suffering mount, have no thought of renouncing and long only for pleasure; the higher ones, whenever pleasure comes, look to the pain in it and do not cling to it.
60.nuance: It reworks 54 almost line for line, but where 54 has the wise leave household life, this has them refuse attachment as each pleasure arrives: a discipline inside experience rather than a change of state.

links.note: Both make good fortune last only as long as the merit behind it: in 51 evil returns when good deeds are exhausted, and in 93 wealth leaves when the deeds that sent it run out (வினையுலந்தக்கால்).
Mudaliar quotes Kural 266 here: those who do austerity do their own work (தங்கருமம்), and the rest waste themselves. 52 names the waste as endless scholarship.

Kural 397 asks why anyone stays unlearned until death. 52 calls lifelong study of grammar and astrology madness. They are compatible only if the Kural's learning is not the instrumental lore 52 mocks; read together, 52 limits which study is worth a life.
Mudaliar points to 135, where learning has no shore and life is short, so one must choose what to learn. 52 draws the harder conclusion that endless study is folly when death is near.
Both urge renouncing while there is time: 342 says renounce while it is still possible, and 53 has the wise renounce without delay once they see that everything fails to last.

Kural 46 asks what one would gain by leaving a household life lived in virtue. 54 says the wise, seeing the pain in household pleasure, keep off the household way. Both answer whether household life is a path the wise should stay on, and they answer opposite ways. The conflict holds unless 54 is read as describing only the fools' pleasure-seeking household, not a virtuous one.
Both press for the good before the body fails: 335 says do good before the death-rattle stops the tongue, and 55 urges the heart to set out now that youth is gone and age and disease are near.

Kural 52 says a household is nothing if the wife lacks household excellence. 56 starts from the same case and adds that she can't be put away, then draws a conclusion the Kural never draws: marriage itself is to be shunned.
Both make hardship the test of austerity: 267 has the ascetic shine like gold in the fire, and 57 counts as blessed only those who hold their vows when unbearable troubles strike.
Parimelazhagar glosses the pity of Kural 157 (நோநொந்து) by quoting this quatrain: grieving that the wrongdoer may fall into the fiery hell.
Both make control of the five senses the way to release: 24 calls the one who guards the five with firmness a seed for the highest ground, and 59 says the one who steers their craving reaches வீடு.
The two share a line and an argument. 54 ends with leaving household life and 60 with refusing to cling to pleasure as it comes.

Both tie freedom from pain to not craving pleasure: 629 says one who does not want the pleasure within pleasure feels no pain within pain, and 60 has the higher ones see the pain in each pleasure and let it go.

new_concepts.gloss: release; liberation from the cycle of births
new_concepts.label_source: The verses use the Tamil word (59: வீடு பெறும்).

source_issues: 60: Mudaliar's commentary breaks off after 'மற்று,'. Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
51-60: Shanmuganar's notes carry the numbers 111-120, apparently from an edition that orders the chapters differently; the content matches these quatrains.
